::: {.hero-section}

# Someone wrote this down for a reason. {.hero-title}

For more than fifty years, the people who grow plants for a botanical garden have been
recording their processes on small paper cards. Every seed sown, every cutting
stuck, every success and failure, written by hand and filed in a cabinet.

Thousands of cards. Decades of knowledge. Sitting in drawers.

This project reads them.

:::

---

## What are propagation cards?

Every plant production facility needs to document its processes, if only to make 
things more efficient the next time around. This documentation becomes critical 
when the "next time" is twenty years from now, and a completely different person
is doing the work. At the UBCBG Nursery, we handle diverse and sometimes rare material
that might never be collected again. Maximizing the probability of success is imperative. 

Historically, before digital databases, the "accession card" was the primary record
of a plant's existence in the Collection. These were printed in triplicate: the top
copy accompanied the seed packet to the nursery, while the other two remained with
the Collection Technician and the Curator. Because of this historical workflow, the terms
"accession card" and "propagation card" are used interchangeably in this project.

The card follows that material through every physical step at the Nursery: sowing, 
treatment, germination, transplanting. The original intent was that each card act as
a single observation of a single accession, handwritten by the person doing the work.
Over the decades, as cards piled up, workers took to condensing the information.
They created hand-written propagation tables on the cards to allow for rapid comparison
of techniques on identical taxa. Older physical cards whose data was considered
'captured' were often reused as scrap, preserving only the most critical propagation
outcomes.

Today, while modern propagation data was eventually digitized (utilizing IrisBG since 2017),
it is rarely entered directly into a computer on the spot. The Nursery is a messy,
dusty environment where physical cards and pen annotations remain far more practical
than screens. Furthermore, writing on the cards first provides a crucial audit trail.
It allows multiple staff members to execute the physical work at the potting bench
while centralizing the final database entry to maintain strict data hygiene.
Even with modern systems in place, horticulturists reference these older paper cards
when developing protocols to see what has worked in the past, and just as importantly,
what hasn't.

Over time, these cards accumulate into something extraordinary: a complete
record of what an institution has tried. They hold the craft knowledge of generations
of horticulturists.


::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**The quiet crisis.** When experienced propagation staff retire, their
knowledge often leaves with them. The cards remain, but without context they
become harder and harder to interpret. Eventually, someone decides they're
taking up space. Or a natural disaster removes the choice altogether.
:::

## What this project does

The Propagation Card Reader is a tool that takes scanned images of handwritten
propagation cards and extracts structured data from them: species names, dates,
treatments, outcomes, accession numbers. It turns paper into a searchable
database.

It does this using a vision language model, a type of software that can look at
an image and describe what it sees, similar to how a person would read the
card. The model runs entirely on a single laptop. No cloud service, no
subscription, no per-page fee. The card images never leave the building.

## Why this site exists

This is not just documentation for a piece of software. It is an attempt to
explain, accessibly, the ideas behind the technology, and to tell the story of
how it came together.

If you work at a botanical garden and have never touched a line of code, start
with [The Cards](the-cards.qmd). You will recognize what you see.

If you are curious about how a computer reads handwriting, [The
Journey](the-journey.qmd) walks through three attempts to solve that problem,
each one teaching something new.

If you want to understand the technical concepts without a computer science
degree, [How It All Works](concepts.qmd) explains things like "language
model" and "answer space" using the cards as examples.

If you want the numbers, go to [Results](results.qmd). If you want to run it
yourself, go to [Use It](use-it.qmd).

::: {.mission-section}

Every botanical garden has knowledge locked in paper. Herbarium sheets, field
notebooks, accession ledgers, propagation cards. The methods described here
are not limited to one type of record or one institution. A laptop, a scanner,
and an open-weight model: that is all it takes.

[See the code on GitHub](https://github.com/Kkubeck/propagation-card-reader){.btn .btn-outline-success}

:::
